cues.text: Grandma Emma’s house
George Weah was born on 1 October 1966 in Monrovia, the capital city of Liberia.
He grew up in Clara Town, a very poor part of the city.
When George was still a baby, his parents separated.
Lift the roof to see who looked after him.
George was one of thirteen children raised mostly by his grandmother, Emma Klonjlaleh Brown.
In her home, lots of cousins, brothers and sisters grew up together, with very little money but plenty of company.
Families come in many shapes. The people who care for you every day are your family.
The Young Survivors
At fifteen, George began playing for a small club in Clara Town.
Its name was Young Survivors.
In 1982, in his first game, he scored two amazing goals, and that season he scored 34 goals in the fourth division.
Climb the steps.
Each promotion is a step up to a higher league.
In three years with George, Young Survivors went up twice, from the fourth level of Liberian football to the second.
Step by step, the little club from a poor neighbourhood kept climbing.
Where you start is not where you have to stay. Small steps, one after another, can take you a long way.
Left on the bench
Later, George joined Mighty Barrolle, one of the biggest clubs in Liberia.
He scored goals often, but he still was not picked to start most games.
Before he played abroad, he also worked at Liberia’s telephone company, as a switchboard operator.
Slide him off the bench.
In 1986 George moved to a rival club, Invincible Eleven, to get his chance.
In 1987 they won the league, and George was the top scorer and the player of the season.
Being left out hurts, but it doesn’t mean you aren’t good enough. Keep working, and look for a new chance.
Someone who believed
In 1987 George moved to Cameroon, to play for Tonnerre Yaoundé, and scored twice in his first game.
Cameroon’s national coach, Claude Le Roy, noticed him and told Arsène Wenger, the manager of Monaco.
Wenger flew to Africa to watch George play.
Open the door to Monaco.
In 1988 George signed for Monaco, and he has said Wenger was an important influence on his career.
In 1989 he was named African Footballer of the Year, and he took the award home for all of Liberia to celebrate.
When someone believes in you, it can change everything. Remember to thank the people who help you.
One point short
In 1995 George became the first African player to win the Ballon d’Or and FIFA World Player of the Year, and he dedicated the FIFA award to Arsène Wenger.
But his home country, Liberia, was a small football nation, hurt by years of war.
George played for Liberia, later coached the team, and even paid for much of it himself.
Flip the points card.
In qualifying for the 2002 World Cup, Liberia finished just one point short.
George never played at a World Cup, but he did so much for his team.
Sometimes you try your hardest and still fall short. That doesn’t erase all the good you did.
School first
Liberia suffered through long years of war.
During his playing career, George became a Goodwill Ambassador for the United Nations, and he tried to use football to bring happiness to children in Liberia.
Open the school doors.
In 1994 George started a club in Monrovia called Junior Professional.
There was only one rule to join: you had to go to school.
Many of its young players went on to play for Liberia.
In 2004 he won the Arthur Ashe Courage Award for his work.
When life gets better for you, reach back and help others. Learning is a strength that stays with you.
